40 is the new 80 BY JODY DUNCAN This issue marks the 40th anniversary of Cinetex - and, in the realm of magazine publishing, 40 years makes Cinefex a very old lady, indeed. Well-resourced mainstream publications such as Life and Look didn't make it to 40. Niche film-related publications akin to ours, such as Cinefantastique and Starlog, only kept the presses running consistently for 36 and 33 years, respectively. Even the big-money, star-filled Premiere lasted a mere 23 years. So forgive us for being quite proud of our longevity. None of us could have foreseen, when Cinefex 1 was published in 1980, that we would still be here 40 years later - nor could we have predicted how the art, science and industry of visual effects would evolve. Oh, the wonders we have seen! We take great pride in having covered them, on the ground, as they occurred. We were there just as motion control technology was allowing camera moves in heretofore static visual effects shots, when optical gave way to digital compositing, when motion capture enabled the recording and transfer of movement onto animated characters. We were there when actors first had helmet-mounted cameras put 1 / 3 on their heads. We were there when artists and technicians created an ambling stained

It was tempting to make our 40th anniversary issue all about that past - after all, reminiscing is what grand old ladies do. But we quickly discarded the idea as too pat, too self-indulgent, too expected. Instead of looking back, we decided to look forward. We would talk to visual effects supervisors and filmmakers, and though, inevitably, there would be some shuffling down Memory Lane, the focus of our discussions would be the future. What might the next 40 years bring? It was a big idea, but we think we've pulled it off. Inside this issue are exclusive interviews with directors James Cameron, George Lucas, Christopher Nolan and Robert Zemeckis, all of whom have delivered some of the most spectacular and innovative films covered in the pages of Cinefex. We also offer a roundtable discussion of visual effects past, present and future with 21 Academy Award-winning visual effects supervisors. We round out the issue with detailed coverage of The Mandalorian and Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker, which seemed fitting for an anniversary issue of Cinefex. By launching a new era in visual effects, the original Star Wars was, in part, responsible for the magazine's inception, and The Empire Strikes Back graced the covers of both our second and third issues. 2 / 3 I have often remarked that Cinefex is a harsh mistress - and she is. ILLUSIONISTS by Graham Edwards It's been an incredible 40 years since Cinefex was first published. In those four decades, the visual effects industry has changed out of all recognition. Or has it? Tools and techniques have certainly evolved, but have the goals of the cinematic illusionist evolved along with them? How does the past inform the present, and what future lies ahead? To chew over these meaty topics, we invited a group of seasoned visual effects professionals to join us in a free-flowing roundtable discussion. First we would indulge in a little nostalgia for the good old days, before opening things up to explore the ways in which effects techniques have changed over time, discuss current trends and philosophies, and speculate on all those wonders that are yet to come. We had no problem coming up with a list of people we wanted to contact. But our hearts quailed when that list of potential interviewees began to climb into the hundreds. How could we possibly keep a lid on the numbers? At last a solution presented itself. We would take as our starting point films that have won the Academy Award for Best Visual Effects - beginning in 1980, the year Cinefex was first published - and interview a tidy total of 21 key visual effects supervisors from the teams involved. Our heartfelt thanks to all those who came to the party, and our humble apologies to the many hundreds we I / 24 just couldn't fit around the table!

CINEFEX - Wind the clock back 40 years and we immediately find ourselves in a lost world of miniature photography and optical wizardry. Ah, the romance! DENNIS MUREN - It was romantic. You could smell the machines and the paint, you could pick up the models, it was easier to set things up and light them. I definitely miss some of it. RICHARD EDLUND - You were able to look around at what was available to photograph, and come up with peculiar ways to set shots up using miniatures, paintings, animation, high-speed photography, explosions. All those things required a kind of ingenuity that you had to be born with. JOHN BRUND - One day when I was at Industrial Light & Magic, Thaine Morris grabbed me as I was walking down the corridor and said, "Hey, sit in this chair, take these wires and don't let go until I tell you." So there I am, sitting in the center of a stage and above me is a miniature of a spaceship hanging upside-down from the rafters. I hear a camera start with a high-pitched whine, and Thaine says: 'Three! Two! One! Now! I let go the wires, and above me there's a big explosion and all these parts come raining down - and that was the shot where the Reliant gets hit in the nacelle in Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan. Thaine says, "Thanks," and I get up and carry on with whatever it was I was doing. It was that kind of thing every day. LINEFEX - ILM's progression with digital through Terminator 2: Judgment Day to Jurassic Park and beyond has been well documented. What did that journey feel like from the inside? STEPHEN ROSENBAUM - I remember ILM announcing this plan to transition artists from traditional roles into the computer graphics department. It was genius, because, now, we had the opportunity to take these expert craftspeople and integrate them into computer graphics. We taught them the tools while they taught us the craft. DENNIS MUREN - During that time, I came to understand a lot of the CG people hadn't studied reality to the level we all had in visual effects. All those years I'd spent doing models or hiking around Yosemite or watching the beach at sunset - I found 1 could apply all that. I could look at a CG image, and say, "I think I know what's wrong with this." I could do that because I knew what 'real' was supposed to look like. MIKE FINK - You know, people remember The Abyss and Jurassic Park, but they forget that in between was Batman Returns. At the same time, it was fascinating and great fun, because of the kind of visual effects I was able to dream up and because of my staff, most of whom were smarter than I was. I wouldn't trade that time for anything, even the heartaches. MIKE FINK - The advent of digital completely disrupted the pricing and labor structure of the visual effects business. Everyone who made hardware or software was excited about having their products used on motion pictures and television, so they would provide them for free. As a consequence, none of us knew how much it actually cost to do the work. We couldn't even predict what the labor cost would be because everything had to be developed from scratch for every show. CINEFEX - What was it like to actually put shots together? MIKE FINK - It was real pick-andshovel work. This was back in the command line days. How much better it would be for all of the creatives - the director, actors, art department, camera and visual effects crews - if full environments could always be there, in camera. Unfortunately, movie schedules and budgets most often preclude the building of full sets or the transporting of huge production crews to locations - especially to those locations exotic enough to simulate alien worlds.
